seoTitle: How to Get a 30-Day Free Trial on TradingView Premium
metaDescription: Find out how to activate a 30-day TradingView free trial for Pro, Pro+, or Premium, plus eligibility rules and how to cancel before billing starts.
intro: TradingView's free plan is usable, but the extra indicators, faster data, and advanced chart layouts all sit behind Pro, Pro+, and Premium — and the fastest way to test whether they're worth paying for is the trial period offered right on the pricing page. This guide walks through where that trial actually starts, what the plan tiers cost once billing kicks in, and the account step you have to clear before TradingView lets you in. It also covers the eligibility limits that can quietly block a trial and why watching the billing date matters as much as activating the trial itself.

steps.heading: Start from TradingView's pricing page
steps.body: The trial isn't hidden in a settings menu — it begins at tradingview.com/pricing, the same page anyone lands on to compare paid tiers. TradingView lays out four levels here: Essential, Plus, Premium, and Ultimate, each shown as a monthly rate billed annually, with the annual toggle saving up to 17% over paying month to month. Before starting a trial, it's worth knowing which tier you're actually testing, since the trial gives you a taste of whichever plan you select on this screen, not a blanket preview of every feature at once.

image.caption: TradingView's pricing page, showing the Essential, Plus, Premium, and Ultimate tiers with annual billing selected and their monthly rates listed.

steps.heading: Compare the tiers before you commit to one
steps.body: Essential and Plus are aimed at casual chart-watchers, while Premium and Ultimate unlock the deeper toolset — more indicators per chart, extra alerts, and priority data — that active or day traders tend to actually use. Pick the tier that matches the features you want to test, not the cheapest one, since switching mid-trial or discovering the plan you picked doesn't include what you needed defeats the point of trying before you buy.

steps.heading: Finish creating or signing into your TradingView account
steps.body: Selecting a plan routes you into account setup if you're not already signed in. TradingView asks for a username here, with an option to opt into marketing emails and a required checkbox agreeing to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy before the Next button becomes active. If you already have a free TradingView account, log into that one instead of creating a second account, since your trial and any existing chart layouts or watchlists should stay attached to a single profile.

image.caption: TradingView's account setup screen, asking for a username and requiring agreement to the Terms of Use before continuing.

steps.heading: Add a payment method to activate the trial
steps.body: Like most subscription trials, TradingView requires a card or PayPal on file before the 30 days start, even though nothing is charged immediately. This is the step people skip expecting a truly no-commitment trial, then are surprised later — the trial is free, but it's a free-then-convert model, not a pass that expires with nothing on record. Treat entering payment details as the actual trigger that starts your countdown.

steps.heading: Know the eligibility rules that can block a trial
steps.body: Trials are typically limited to accounts that haven't already used one on that tier, so a second attempt on the same email or account often won't qualify, regardless of how long ago the first trial ran. If the trial option doesn't appear or gets rejected during checkout, check whether the account has any trial history before assuming it's a bug — TradingView enforces this per account, not per browser or device.

steps.heading: Use the 30 days to actually test premium features
steps.body: Once active, spend the trial deliberately: add the extra indicators to a real chart you use, set up the alerts you'd rely on day to day, and check whether the faster data feed changes anything for your trading style. Treating the trial as a real workflow test rather than just clicking through settings is what tells you whether the paid tier earns its monthly cost.

steps.heading: Cancel before billing starts if you don't want to continue
steps.body: The trial converts automatically into a paid subscription at the end of 30 days unless you cancel first, so mark the date rather than relying on a reminder email. Cancellation happens from your account's subscription settings, and doing it a day or two early is safer than waiting until the last hour, in case of any processing delay on TradingView's end.

faq.question: Does TradingView offer a 30-day free trial in 2026?
faq.answer: Yes, TradingView offers a 30-day trial for its paid plans, started directly from the pricing page, though eligibility rules apply to accounts that have used a trial before.

faq.question: Will I be charged automatically after the trial ends?
faq.answer: Yes, unless you cancel before the trial period ends, billing typically starts automatically using the payment method you added to activate the trial.

faq.question: What features are unlocked during the trial?
faq.answer: Whichever paid tier you selected on the pricing page — Essential, Plus, Premium, or Ultimate — determines what you get, from extra indicators to faster data and more alerts.

faq.question: What might block me from getting the free trial?
faq.answer: Having already used a trial on that account is the most common blocker; TradingView generally limits trials to one per account per tier rather than per device.

faq.question: Do I need a credit card to start the TradingView trial?
faq.answer: Yes, a card or PayPal account is required to activate the trial even though you aren't charged until the 30 days end, so cancelling on time is what keeps it free.
